newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda reopens genocide trial of key suspect.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda reopens genocide trial of key suspect.

text.p: Rwanda reopened on Wednesday the trial of a prominent politician accused of being a ringleader in the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis -- despite being born a Tutsi.

Froduald Karamira, former vice-president of the Hutu extremist MDR-Power party under the ousted Hutu government, is charged with genocide and crimes against humanity and is the most senior genocide suspect to come to trial in Rwanda.
Karamira was born a Tutsi but changed to Hutu using a centuries-old custom which allows people to change tribe.
He is charged under Rwanda's genocide law with Category One crimes and therefore will face the death penalty if convicted.
Wearing Rwanda's pink prison uniform, Karamira was led handcuffed into Kigali's packed Nyamirambo Court when his trial resumed on Wednesday following an adjournment since January 14.
"As a politican, I would say I have no confidence in the system of justice here. As a man I would say the same thing as well," Karamira told Reuters.
"I wish they would finish it today but this process is so slow I think it will carry on," he said.

Plaintiffs, Rwandan Patriotic Army soldiers, legal officials, guards, journalists and human rights workers packed the courtroom, while outside several hundred Rwandans tuned into the proceedings which were broadcast live on state radio.
Karamira was jeered after his last court appearance when his defence lawyer requested an adjournment.
Eighteen civilian plaintiffs were waiting to be cross-examined in the court on Wednesday.

Karamira is accused of being a leader of the Hutu extremist Interahamwe militia, one of the main forces that carried out the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates. He was allegedly responsible for inciting genocide through broadcasts on state-run Radio Rwanda and Radio Mille Collines.
He was arrested at Ethiopia's Addis Ababa airport last June and extradited to Rwanda.
At least nine people have been sentenced to death for genocide since trials of the first of some 90,000 suspects crammed into Rwanda's jails started in late December.
The United Nations has an international criminal tribunal for the Rwandan genocide with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. It has 11 suspects in custody at its Tanzania headquarters.
Last week Theoneste Bagosora, widely regarded as the most wanted suspect in detention, was transferred from Cameroon to the tribunal's headquarters along with three other accused.
Bagosora was cabinet director in the defence ministry at the start of the genocide and is accused of directing events in the first days of the killings.
